narrative:
The model determined that you have a 98% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process heavily weighs this predicted outcome, your law school application was rejected.

The three factors that most strongly drove this decision were, in order: your class ranking in your third year of law school, your LSAT score, and your first-year class ranking. Each of these pushed the prediction strongly toward failure rather than success.

Your third-year ranking placed you in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average student who is admitted. This was the single biggest reason the model expected you to struggle on the bar. Your LSAT score of 25 was also well below the average of 37 among accepted students, adding further weight toward a failing outcome. Finally, your first-year ranking in the lowest decile—compared to an average around the sixth decile for accepted applicants—reinforced the same concern about your academic preparation.

Your low undergraduate GPA of 1.8 (versus an average of 3.23) and middle family income bracket also contributed, though less dramatically. The fact that you plan to attend full-time, which is common among accepted students, did not offset these academic signals.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your foundational skills before retaking the LSAT or reapplying. Consider targeted bar-prep courses, additional coursework to raise your academic record, or waiting until you can demonstrate clearer evidence of readiness. Many students successfully reapply after addressing these exact gaps.
